title: Smoke wagon slang and the first time he heard the word jazz
summary: He defines 'smoke wagon' and says ragtime gave way to the word jazz that he cannot trace.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I was gonna ask you about a couple of words. You said a guy had a big smoke wagon?

Yeah, pistol. That's what you call a pistol? Yeah, big long things. What they used to do, it used to be, the police used to carry it mostly. It was a .38. It was built on a .41 frame. So it was, it had about a seven, eight inch barrel, you see. And the thing was big long to stick it down in here like that, you see. They call it smoke wagon.
I was gonna ask you about the word jazz, too. When did you first hear that?
Well, there's so many different versions of that. A lot of people say J-A-S-S. The first I ever heard of it was J-A-Z-Z, the way it is now.
Was that before the war or after the war?
Well, that's before. What do you mean? World War I. Well, no, where you at, my boy? Where you putting me? I wasn't in World War I, I was in World War II.
11 years old. Yeah, but I mean, did you hear the word when you were a kid? Did you ever use it?
Well, no, the first thing, ragtime, they did ratty, used to call it ratty music. And then all of a sudden up cropped this word jazz. Now, behind it originated, you got me.
And you don't remember the ear of the word jazz?
